name: Palatal expander

lead: A palatal expander widens the upper jaw by turning a screw in a fixed device, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18, to correct a narrow palate, crossbite and crowding. In looksmaxxing communities, expanders and MARPE are discussed for a broader smile and fuller midface, often alongside mewing.

Screw turns separate the two halves of the palate; new bone fills the gap and a retention period follows. Types include rapid (RME), slow, mini-implant-assisted (MARPE) and surgically assisted (SARPE) expansion. Trials focus on dental and airway outcomes in children; broader facial change in adults has not been tested in the sources reviewed.

paras: An orthodontist fits the device and the screw is turned on a set schedule, followed by months of retention. Older patients may use MARPE or surgical versions.
Speech changes, pain, a gap between front teeth, bone thinning and relapse are reported; MARPE and SARPE involve implants or surgery.

angle.text: A palatal expander widens the upper jaw, giving a broader dental arch and smile; in kids it is established orthodontics, and some adults hope for a fuller midface, sometimes alongside mewing. Facial change in adults has not been tested.

lead: A palatal expander is an orthodontic device used to widen the upper jaw so that upper and lower teeth fit together better, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18 [1]. Types include rapid maxillary expansion (RME), slow expansion, mini-implant-assisted expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) [1].

Orthodontic indications include a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower, posterior crossbite, cleft palate and crowding [1]. In looksmaxxing communities, expanders and MARPE are discussed as ways to widen the palate or change the face, often alongside mewing. Published trials focus on dental and airway outcomes in children, and evidence for broader facial change in adults is not established in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Speech changes, pain, gap between front teeth, relapse [1]

paras: In rapid expansion a central screw is turned, typically about 0.5 to 1 mm a day, until a crossbite is corrected, and the device stays in for roughly three to six months while bone fills the gap, followed by retention [1]. Slow expansion turns about 1 mm per week [1]. MARPE anchors the appliance to the palatal bone with two to four mini-implants and is described as usable in young adults whose suture has fused; SARPE involves a surgeon cutting the suture [1].

Emerson C. Angell published the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860, after placing a screw in a 14-year-old patient [1]. Later developments include the Haas expander (1956), the Hyrax (1968) and the quad helix (1975) [1].

A meta-analysis of early correction of functional posterior crossbite found the quad helix more effective than expansion plates at increasing intermolar width, with greater relapse at about 5.6 years post-treatment. A randomised trial compared tooth-borne with tooth-bone-borne RME appliances over five years, and another compared clear aligners with RME in mixed dentition.

A systematic review reported that RME reduced the apnea-hypopnea index in children but rated the evidence low to very low and did not suggest it as an elective sleep apnea treatment. A network meta-analysis found RME alone was not associated with a significant AHI reduction, while combinations with adenotonsillectomy or mandibular advancement were. A randomised trial has compared RME with adenotonsillectomy.

Reported problems include speech difficulty, pain and headache, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth, bone thinning and relapse; older studies suggest a third to half of expansion may be lost before stabilising [1].

looksmax.org threads ask whether an expander is worthwhile for a narrow or crowded palate [2][3], whether it can widen the mandible [4], and how it pairs with mewing [5]. One reply summarised rapid expansion as roughly 0.5 mm of widening a day over three to six months [3].
Randomised and meta-analytic studies concern children's crossbite, appliance comparison and sleep-disordered breathing. No studies found of palatal expanders for facial aesthetics in adults.
